appellations.grapes: Garganega (at least 70%), Trebbiano di Soave, up to 30% together with other white grapes
appellations.summary: The name evolved from 'pontara', dialect for a climb. Ponsara links the flat floor of the Val Ponsara with the slopes of Foscarino, Pigno and Froscà in a harmonious amphitheatre facing north-east and south-east, with gentle gradients of 5 to 20%. Dark volcanic clay loam over redder silty loam; sheltered by Foscarino to the north and Froscà to the south, it is cool and relatively rainy.
appellations.terroir: 110.5 ha in total, 63.5 ha of vines (58%); slope and foot facing south and south-east, 40 to 130 m.
appellations.classification: UGA (unità geografica aggiuntiva) of Soave: one of 33 named areas in Annex A of the Soave DOC rules, approved in 2019 (usable from that vintage). The same names may be used for Soave DOC, Soave Superiore DOCG and Recioto di Soave DOCG when all the grapes come from inside the UGA. A place name, not a quality rank.

appellations.name: Froscà
appellations.grapes: Garganega (at least 70%), Trebbiano di Soave, up to 30% together with other white grapes
appellations.summary: One of the most historic crus of Soave Classico, almost surrounded by other UGAs. Its soil is mainly volcanic with some limestone outcrops, brownish-yellow to greyish-brown clay with scattered basalt; vines on small terraces held by dry-stone walls or ciglioni on slopes of 10 to 30% include very old plants, some 90 to 100 years. Gini's Soave Classico La Froscà, from about 6 ha owned in the cru, is the reference.
appellations.terroir: 42.2 ha in total, 33.5 ha of vines (79%, the highest share of any UGA); summits and slopes facing south and south-east, 40 to 160 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Froscà has the highest proportion of land under vine of all 33 UGAs, 79%.
appellations.classification: UGA (unità geografica aggiuntiva) of Soave: one of 33 named areas in Annex A of the Soave DOC rules, approved in 2019 (usable from that vintage). The same names may be used for Soave DOC, Soave Superiore DOCG and Recioto di Soave DOCG when all the grapes come from inside the UGA. A place name, not a quality rank.

appellations.name: Volpare
appellations.grapes: Garganega (at least 70%), Trebbiano di Soave, up to 30% together with other white grapes
appellations.summary: One of the smallest UGAs, historically linked to Froscà and similar in soil and altitude, but facing more to the south-west and dotted with groves, olive and cherry trees. The name comes from caves in the limestone that sheltered foxes (volpi), which are returning to the Classico. Monte Riondo dominates the view; temperatures are average and rainfall modest.
appellations.terroir: 28.3 ha in total, 13.4 ha of vines (47%); summits and slopes facing south and south-east, 40 to 160 m.
appellations.classification: UGA (unità geografica aggiuntiva) of Soave: one of 33 named areas in Annex A of the Soave DOC rules, approved in 2019 (usable from that vintage). The same names may be used for Soave DOC, Soave Superiore DOCG and Recioto di Soave DOCG when all the grapes come from inside the UGA. A place name, not a quality rank.

appellations.name: Tenda
appellations.grapes: Garganega (at least 70%), Trebbiano di Soave, up to 30% together with other white grapes
appellations.summary: A large UGA in the Classico hills, mostly summits and upper slopes facing south and west.
appellations.terroir: 271.7 ha in total, 93.3 ha of vines (34%); summits and slopes facing south and west, 70 to 170 m.
appellations.classification: UGA (unità geografica aggiuntiva) of Soave: one of 33 named areas in Annex A of the Soave DOC rules, approved in 2019 (usable from that vintage). The same names may be used for Soave DOC, Soave Superiore DOCG and Recioto di Soave DOCG when all the grapes come from inside the UGA. A place name, not a quality rank.

appellations.name: Croce
appellations.grapes: Garganega (at least 70%), Trebbiano di Soave, up to 30% together with other white grapes
appellations.summary: A small UGA of the Classico on the lower slopes and foot of the hills, facing south and south-west.
appellations.terroir: 42.7 ha in total, 26.4 ha of vines (62%); slope and foot facing south and south-west, 70 to 120 m.
appellations.classification: UGA (unità geografica aggiuntiva) of Soave: one of 33 named areas in Annex A of the Soave DOC rules, approved in 2019 (usable from that vintage). The same names may be used for Soave DOC, Soave Superiore DOCG and Recioto di Soave DOCG when all the grapes come from inside the UGA. A place name, not a quality rank.

appellations.name: Zoppega
appellations.grapes: Garganega (at least 70%), Trebbiano di Soave, up to 30% together with other white grapes
appellations.summary: The name perhaps describes the limping, up-and-down skyline of the hill seen from the south (zoppo, lame); Zoppega marks the edge of the Classico on this side. Deep silty-clay soils are basaltic to the east and increasingly calcareous to the west, where dry-stone walls multiply. Paleontologists have long studied traces of prehistoric communities here. Its almost exclusively southern aspect weighs on the wines in very hot years.
appellations.terroir: 96.7 ha in total, 51.8 ha of vines (54%); summits and slopes facing south and south-east, 30 to 100 m.
appellations.classification: UGA (unità geografica aggiuntiva) of Soave: one of 33 named areas in Annex A of the Soave DOC rules, approved in 2019 (usable from that vintage). The same names may be used for Soave DOC, Soave Superiore DOCG and Recioto di Soave DOCG when all the grapes come from inside the UGA. A place name, not a quality rank.

appellations.name: Ca' del Vento
appellations.grapes: Garganega (at least 70%), Trebbiano di Soave, up to 30% together with other white grapes
appellations.summary: The smallest UGA, once also called Monticello, is the last spur of the Classico hills in Monteforte d'Alpone. Its basalt soils are dark brown, silty clay and neutral at the surface, redder and weakly acid below, with altered to compact basalt between 50 and 100 cm. 'House of the wind' describes its exposure to air from the upper Alpone valley.
appellations.terroir: 31.3 ha in total, 9.8 ha of vines (31%); low summits and slopes facing south and east, 30 to 45 m.
appellations.classification: UGA (unità geografica aggiuntiva) of Soave: one of 33 named areas in Annex A of the Soave DOC rules, approved in 2019 (usable from that vintage). The same names may be used for Soave DOC, Soave Superiore DOCG and Recioto di Soave DOCG when all the grapes come from inside the UGA. A place name, not a quality rank.

appellations.name: Broia
appellations.grapes: Garganega (at least 70%), Trebbiano di Soave, up to 30% together with other white grapes
appellations.summary: One of three UGAs in the limestone west of the Soave DOC, outside the Classico, in the commune of Mezzane di Sotto. It sits on the terraced alluvial fans of the Mezzane torrent at about 120 m, almost flat, with extremely calcareous, moderately alkaline soils. Cool air from the Lessinia mountains moderates temperatures, but rainfall is low and the soils hold little water, so relief irrigation matters. The name may derive from the Celtic 'brolo', a walled garden or orchard.
appellations.terroir: 372.8 ha in total, 52.7 ha of vines (14%); foot of slope facing south, about 100 to 120 m. Calcareous alluvial fans.
appellations.classification: UGA (unità geografica aggiuntiva) of Soave: one of 33 named areas in Annex A of the Soave DOC rules, approved in 2019 (usable from that vintage). The same names may be used for Soave DOC, Soave Superiore DOCG and Recioto di Soave DOCG when all the grapes come from inside the UGA. A place name, not a quality rank.

appellations.name: Paradiso
appellations.grapes: Garganega (at least 70%), Trebbiano di Soave, up to 30% together with other white grapes
appellations.summary: A western, non-Classico UGA on the terraced fans of the Lessinia torrents, among channel deposits. The soils are extremely calcareous to about 50 cm, dark yellowish brown and gravelly, becoming very stony with depth; permeability is high and water reserves poor, and rooting depth is limited to 50 to 100 cm by the stones. It is the clearest case in Soave of a gravel terroir rather than a hillside one.
appellations.terroir: 156.8 ha in total, 43.9 ha of vines (28%); flat land facing south-west, about 100 m. Calcareous alluvial gravels.
appellations.classification: UGA (unità geografica aggiuntiva) of Soave: one of 33 named areas in Annex A of the Soave DOC rules, approved in 2019 (usable from that vintage). The same names may be used for Soave DOC, Soave Superiore DOCG and Recioto di Soave DOCG when all the grapes come from inside the UGA. A place name, not a quality rank.

appellations.name: Monte di Colognola
appellations.grapes: Garganega (at least 70%), Trebbiano di Soave, up to 30% together with other white grapes
appellations.summary: A large UGA covering the hills of Colognola ai Colli in the west of the DOC, including the Colli Scaligeri subzone. On the slopes the soils are deep and formed on stratified marine limestone, clayey and moderately alkaline; on the hilltops everything changes to basalt-derived clay over sandier subsoil. Rainfall is below average, temperatures normal, with wider day-night swings near harvest.
appellations.terroir: 1,808 ha in total, 434 ha of vines (24%); summits and foot slopes facing south-west to east, around 100 m and above.
appellations.classification: UGA (unità geografica aggiuntiva) of Soave: one of 33 named areas in Annex A of the Soave DOC rules, approved in 2019 (usable from that vintage). The same names may be used for Soave DOC, Soave Superiore DOCG and Recioto di Soave DOCG when all the grapes come from inside the UGA. A place name, not a quality rank.

appellations.name: Duello
appellations.grapes: Garganega (at least 70%), Trebbiano di Soave, up to 30% together with other white grapes
appellations.summary: Monte Duello rises in the middle of the Val d'Alpone east of the Classico, a very homogeneous and historic area with views back over the eastern Classico and across to the volcanic cones of Monte Crocetta and Monte Calvarina at Roncà. Its soils are entirely volcanic, deep, greyish-brown silty clay on moderately steep slopes, and strong ventilation even in summer widens the day-night swing and keeps grapes healthy.
appellations.terroir: 306.8 ha in total, 110.3 ha of vines (36%); slopes facing south and south-west, 60 to 200 m.
appellations.classification: UGA (unità geografica aggiuntiva) of Soave: one of 33 named areas in Annex A of the Soave DOC rules, approved in 2019 (usable from that vintage). The same names may be used for Soave DOC, Soave Superiore DOCG and Recioto di Soave DOCG when all the grapes come from inside the UGA. A place name, not a quality rank.

appellations.name: Roncà - Monte Calvarina
appellations.grapes: Garganega (at least 70%), Trebbiano di Soave, up to 30% together with other white grapes
appellations.summary: The largest UGA by total area and by vineyard, in the commune of Roncà at the eastern end of the DOC. It faces almost entirely south-west and its vineyards climb past 600 m on the slopes of the Calvarina volcano, the highest in Soave. All the soils come from basalts of various kinds, but depth and slope vary so much that producers get very different wines from similar rock. Fattori, based at Terrossa di Roncà, is a leading estate.
appellations.terroir: 1,617.6 ha in total, 406.5 ha of vines (25%); summits and slopes facing south and south-west, 90 to 600 m.
appellations.nerd_note: At up to 600 m, Monte Calvarina holds the highest vineyards of Soave, more than 200 m above anything in the Classico.
appellations.classification: UGA (unità geografica aggiuntiva) of Soave: one of 33 named areas in Annex A of the Soave DOC rules, approved in 2019 (usable from that vintage). The same names may be used for Soave DOC, Soave Superiore DOCG and Recioto di Soave DOCG when all the grapes come from inside the UGA. A place name, not a quality rank.

appellations.name: Soave Classico
appellations.grapes: Garganega (at least 70%), Trebbiano di Soave, up to 30% together with other white grapes
appellations.summary:
The historic heart of Soave: the hills of Soave and Monteforte d'Alpone recognised in October 1931 as the first delimited zone for a 'vino tipico' in Italy, after a first protection measure in 1924 and the founding of the producers' consortium. That 1931 line, starting and ending at the Verona gate of Soave's medieval walls, became the Soave Classico DOC zone in 1968. A plaque on Soave's Palazzo di Giustizia dated 1375 already regulated the town's wine.

Twenty-eight of the 33 UGAs lie inside it, from the limestone slopes of Costeggiola and Pigno near the town to the basalt hills of Foscarino, Froscà, Monte Grande and Brognoligo toward the Alpone. The Castelvero fault splits the zone into a calcareous west and a volcanic east, and the Veronese pergola still dominates. Classico wines must be made and bottled inside the zone (with exceptions for the province of Verona).

Pieropan (Calvarino, La Rocca), Inama, Gini, Prà, Suavia, Coffele, Filippi, Ca' Rugate and Cantina del Castello are among the defining producers; the Cantina di Soave cooperative handles a large share of the grapes.
appellations.terroir: Hills of Soave and Monteforte d'Alpone between about 40 and 380 m; Eocene basalts and tuffs east of the Castelvero fault, marine limestone to the west; mild climate with high rainfall in the north.
appellations.nerd_note: Soave claims the first legally delimited wine zone in Italy: the ministerial decree of 23 October 1931, published in the Gazzetta Ufficiale of 16 December 1931.
appellations.classification: 'Classico' mention of the Soave DOC (and of Soave Superiore and Recioto di Soave DOCG), reserved for the zone of the 1931 decree in the communes of Soave and Monteforte d'Alpone.

appellations.name: Soave Colli Scaligeri
appellations.village: San Martino Buon Albergo, Lavagno, Mezzane di Sotto, Illasi, Colognola ai Colli, Cazzano di Tramigna, Montecchia di Crosara, Roncà and others
appellations.grapes: Garganega (at least 70%), Trebbiano di Soave, up to 30% together with other white grapes
appellations.summary: The hillside subzone of Soave outside the Classico: the slopes of the Lessini foothills from Marcellise (San Martino Buon Albergo) east through Lavagno, the Mezzane and Illasi valleys, Colognola ai Colli and on toward the Alpone, drawn along the line where hill meets plain. The name honours the Scaligeri, the della Scala lords of Verona whose castles crown Soave and other hill towns. Colli Scaligeri wines must be vinified inside the delimited zone (with some exceptions within the province), carry a vintage, and come from lower yields than plain Soave (14 t/ha). Several UGAs (Monte di Colognola, Broia, Paradiso, Duello, Roncà-Monte Calvarina) lie in or next to it.
appellations.terroir: Hills from about 50 to 600 m on limestone in the west and basalt in the east (Roncà, Montecchia), above the alluvial plain of the Adige tributaries.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of the Soave DOC ('Soave' Colli Scaligeri) with its own delimitation in article 3 of the disciplinare.

appellations.name: Modigliana
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese (at least 95% for a sottozona wine)
appellations.summary:
Modigliana is the highest and coolest of Romagna's sottozone, the whole commune at the head of three valleys (Ibola, Acerreta and Tramazzo) in the Apennine foothills. Until 1923 it belonged to Tuscany, and its Sangiovese has something Tuscan about it: taut, austere and long-lived (the disciplinare speaks of firm structure, power and longevity), from the marnoso-arenacea, the sandstone and marl flysch of the northern Apennines, rather than the clays and spungone further down.

A group of growers (Villa Papiano, Il Pratello, Torre San Martino, Mutiliana and others) has made it the most talked-about name in Romagna. The rules are strict: new vineyards need 4,000 vines per hectare, yields stop at 9 t/ha, normal Modigliana may not be sold before 1 September after the harvest, the Riserva not before 1 September of the third year. There is also a Romagna Bianco Modigliana (Trebbiano with up to 40% Chardonnay and Sauvignon).
appellations.terroir: The whole commune of Modigliana, vineyards from about 150 to 600 m; marnoso-arenacea flysch (sandstone and marl), poor and well drained; cooler and later than the rest of Romagna.
appellations.nerd_note: Modigliana's three valleys, Ibola, Acerreta and Tramazzo, are increasingly named on labels as a further level of detail.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Romagna DOC, one of 16 now listed (the original 12 of 2011 plus Imola, Coriano, San Clemente and Verucchio; San Vicinio has become Mercato Saraceno). A Romagna Sangiovese with a sottozona name needs at least 95% Sangiovese, at most 9 t/ha and 12.5% potential alcohol (13% for Riserva). The Riserva is released only from 1 September of the third year after the harvest, with two months in bottle documented.

appellations.name: Predappio
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese (at least 95% for a sottozona wine)
appellations.summary: The whole commune of Predappio in the Rabbi valley, south of Forlì. Its slopes of clay and marl with sandstone layers, and a local long-berried biotype of Sangiovese, give very fruity wines with firm, rather austere tannins, as the disciplinare describes them. Fattoria Nicolucci at Predappio Alta, whose Vigna del Generale is one of Romagna's classic Riservas, and Noelia Ricci at the Pandolfa estate lead.
appellations.terroir: Whole commune of Predappio; clay, marl and sandstone hills of the Rabbi valley, about 150 to 450 m.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Romagna DOC, one of 16 now listed (the original 12 of 2011 plus Imola, Coriano, San Clemente and Verucchio; San Vicinio has become Mercato Saraceno). A Romagna Sangiovese with a sottozona name needs at least 95% Sangiovese, at most 9 t/ha and 12.5% potential alcohol (13% for Riserva). The Riserva is released only from 1 September of the third year after the harvest, with two months in bottle documented.

appellations.name: Bertinoro
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese (at least 95% for a sottozona wine)
appellations.summary: Bertinoro, the 'balcony of Romagna', is the hill town above Forlimpopoli whose slopes are built on spungone, a yellowish, fossil-rich calcareous sandstone of marine origin. The sottozona's Sangiovese is warm, powerful and saline. Bertinoro also has its own Pagadebit ('pays the debts', from Bombino Bianco). Fattoria Paradiso, Tenuta La Viola, Giovanna Madonia and Celli are among its producers. Bertinoro was traditionally Albana country, and the disciplinare notes that its Sangiovese, discovered more recently, has an important structure that needs fairly long ageing; the poor, calcareous spungone soils also explain the area's affinity for Albana and Bombino Bianco.
appellations.terroir: Hills around Bertinoro above the Via Emilia; spungone (calcareous fossil sandstone) and clays, about 100 to 300 m, with sea influence.
appellations.nerd_note: Bertinoro's iron 'column of hospitality' in the main square had rings for each noble family; travellers who tied up their horse were guests of that house.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Romagna DOC, one of 16 now listed (the original 12 of 2011 plus Imola, Coriano, San Clemente and Verucchio; San Vicinio has become Mercato Saraceno). A Romagna Sangiovese with a sottozona name needs at least 95% Sangiovese, at most 9 t/ha and 12.5% potential alcohol (13% for Riserva). The Riserva is released only from 1 September of the third year after the harvest, with two months in bottle documented.

appellations.name: Brisighella
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese (at least 95% for a sottozona wine)
appellations.summary: Parts of Brisighella, Faenza and Casola Valsenio in the Lamone valley, where the Vena del Gesso, a long ridge of gypsum, crosses the Apennine foothills. Its sottozona covers Sangiovese and also a Romagna Bianco, and any form of enrichment is forbidden. According to the disciplinare, its particular microclimate also sustains an important olive-oil tradition (Brisighella has its own DOP oil), and the soils near the gypsum ridge, rich in sandstone and clay, give structured, elegant wines with marked floral and fruity notes and good freshness.
appellations.terroir: Lamone valley hills: calcareous clays, spungone and gypsum near the Vena del Gesso, about 100 to 500 m.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Romagna DOC, one of 16 now listed (the original 12 of 2011 plus Imola, Coriano, San Clemente and Verucchio; San Vicinio has become Mercato Saraceno). A Romagna Sangiovese with a sottozona name needs at least 95% Sangiovese, at most 9 t/ha and 12.5% potential alcohol (13% for Riserva). The Riserva is released only from 1 September of the third year after the harvest, with two months in bottle documented.

appellations.name: Marzeno
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese (at least 95% for a sottozona wine)
appellations.summary: The Marzeno valley south of Faenza, between the Lamone and Montone valleys. Fattoria Zerbina, whose Pietramora Riserva helped relaunch Romagna Sangiovese in the 1990s, is the reference estate. The disciplinare notes that Marzeno has the first major outcrop of the spungone, the fossil-rich calcareous sandstone that is interbedded here with the blue Plio-Pleistocene clays: rugged land that gives strong wines in which fruit dominates over flowers.
appellations.terroir: Clay and marl hills of the Marzeno valley, about 100 to 350 m.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Romagna DOC, one of 16 now listed (the original 12 of 2011 plus Imola, Coriano, San Clemente and Verucchio; San Vicinio has become Mercato Saraceno). A Romagna Sangiovese with a sottozona name needs at least 95% Sangiovese, at most 9 t/ha and 12.5% potential alcohol (13% for Riserva). The Riserva is released only from 1 September of the third year after the harvest, with two months in bottle documented.

appellations.name: Oriolo
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese (at least 95% for a sottozona wine)
appellations.summary: The hills of Oriolo dei Fichi above Faenza, crowned by the 15th-century hexagonal Torre di Oriolo. Besides Sangiovese, the sottozona protects Centesimino, a local aromatic red grape (also called Savignôn rosso) made as a red, Riserva, passito and sparkling rosé. The disciplinare singles out its yellow sands, which surface among clay or silty-clay soils: depending on exposure and the balance of sand and clay, Oriolo gives either structured wines that need time to soften or fruity, floral wines ready sooner.
appellations.terroir: Low hills above Faenza between the Lamone and Montone, clays and sands, about 100 to 250 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Centesimino survived in a single Faenza garden and was named after Pietro Pianori, nicknamed 'Centesimino', who propagated it after phylloxera.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Romagna DOC, one of 16 now listed (the original 12 of 2011 plus Imola, Coriano, San Clemente and Verucchio; San Vicinio has become Mercato Saraceno). A Romagna Sangiovese with a sottozona name needs at least 95% Sangiovese, at most 9 t/ha and 12.5% potential alcohol (13% for Riserva). The Riserva is released only from 1 September of the third year after the harvest, with two months in bottle documented.

appellations.name: Castrocaro
appellations.village: Castrocaro Terme e Terra del Sole, Dovadola, Rocca San Casciano, Forlì
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese (at least 95% for a sottozona wine)
appellations.summary: The Montone valley around the spa town of Castrocaro Terme and Terra del Sole (the Medici's 16th-century ideal fortress town), up to Dovadola and Rocca San Casciano, plus a strip of Forlì. Sangiovese and a Romagna Bianco are allowed, with enrichment forbidden. This is the 'Romagna Toscana', long under the Grand Duchy of Tuscany, and the disciplinare admits that the subzone owes more to history and local tradition than to any real difference from neighbouring Oriolo.
appellations.terroir: Montone valley hills, clays, marl and sandstone, about 100 to 500 m.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Romagna DOC, one of 16 now listed (the original 12 of 2011 plus Imola, Coriano, San Clemente and Verucchio; San Vicinio has become Mercato Saraceno). A Romagna Sangiovese with a sottozona name needs at least 95% Sangiovese, at most 9 t/ha and 12.5% potential alcohol (13% for Riserva). The Riserva is released only from 1 September of the third year after the harvest, with two months in bottle documented.

appellations.name: Meldola
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese (at least 95% for a sottozona wine)
appellations.summary: The Bidente valley around Meldola, adjoining Predappio to the west. A Sangiovese-only sottozona of clay and sandstone hills. The disciplinare notes that the area was farmed in Roman times and that its main exposure, from north-west to north-east, gives fine Sangiovese with a fruity aromatic profile, an unusual case of a subzone defined partly by cool, north-facing slopes.
appellations.terroir: Bidente valley hills around Meldola; clays and sandstone.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Romagna DOC, one of 16 now listed (the original 12 of 2011 plus Imola, Coriano, San Clemente and Verucchio; San Vicinio has become Mercato Saraceno). A Romagna Sangiovese with a sottozona name needs at least 95% Sangiovese, at most 9 t/ha and 12.5% potential alcohol (13% for Riserva). The Riserva is released only from 1 September of the third year after the harvest, with two months in bottle documented.

appellations.name: Cesena
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese (at least 95% for a sottozona wine)
appellations.summary: The hills of the commune of Cesena in the Savio valley, a Sangiovese-only sottozona of clays and marl with sea influence. Cesena's wines were cited by classical Latin authors, the disciplinare recalls, and its Sangiovese combines real but never excessive structure with clear ripe-cherry fruit: structure and elegance together.
appellations.terroir: Savio valley hills south of Cesena; clays and marl, about 50 to 300 m.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Romagna DOC, one of 16 now listed (the original 12 of 2011 plus Imola, Coriano, San Clemente and Verucchio; San Vicinio has become Mercato Saraceno). A Romagna Sangiovese with a sottozona name needs at least 95% Sangiovese, at most 9 t/ha and 12.5% potential alcohol (13% for Riserva). The Riserva is released only from 1 September of the third year after the harvest, with two months in bottle documented.

appellations.name: Longiano
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese (at least 95% for a sottozona wine)
appellations.summary: The hills of Longiano, Montiano and Borghi between the Rubicone and Uso valleys, near the Adriatic. Sangiovese and a Romagna Bianco are allowed. The disciplinare describes warm, rich wines with very evident fruit and good structure, and warns that pushing them toward power sacrifices the natural elegance of grape and place.
appellations.terroir: Low coastal hills, clays and sands, close to the sea.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Romagna DOC, one of 16 now listed (the original 12 of 2011 plus Imola, Coriano, San Clemente and Verucchio; San Vicinio has become Mercato Saraceno). A Romagna Sangiovese with a sottozona name needs at least 95% Sangiovese, at most 9 t/ha and 12.5% potential alcohol (13% for Riserva). The Riserva is released only from 1 September of the third year after the harvest, with two months in bottle documented.

appellations.name: Mercato Saraceno
appellations.village: Mercato Saraceno, Sarsina, Roncofreddo, Sogliano al Rubicone, Cesena
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese (at least 95% for a sottozona wine)
appellations.summary: The upper Savio valley around Mercato Saraceno and Sarsina (birthplace of the Roman playwright Plautus), formerly called San Vicinio after the valley's patron saint. Besides Sangiovese it protects Romagna Famoso, an aromatic white grape revived in this area, also as spumante. The disciplinare calls this the fullest expression of the Romagna marnoso-arenacea formation; the calcareous 'Celincordia' soils (Haplic Calcisols), especially below 150 to 200 m, have proved the best for Sangiovese, giving balanced wines with sweet tannins. Famoso's revival started here around 2000 from two old rows of vines.
appellations.terroir: Upper Savio valley; marl and sandstone hills, up to about 500 m; cooler and more continental.
appellations.nerd_note: The sottozona was renamed from San Vicinio to Mercato Saraceno; old labels with the saint's name come from the same hills.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Romagna DOC, one of 16 now listed (the original 12 of 2011 plus Imola, Coriano, San Clemente and Verucchio; San Vicinio has become Mercato Saraceno). A Romagna Sangiovese with a sottozona name needs at least 95% Sangiovese, at most 9 t/ha and 12.5% potential alcohol (13% for Riserva). The Riserva is released only from 1 September of the third year after the harvest, with two months in bottle documented.

appellations.name: Serra
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese (at least 95% for a sottozona wine)
appellations.summary: The Senio valley between Castel Bolognese and Riolo Terme, at the western end of the Ravenna hills. A Sangiovese-only sottozona. The disciplinare calls Serra a historically prized area with a rather continental climate, little moderated by the distant sea, and wines with delicate floral notes and fresh fruit when the vines are well exposed.
appellations.terroir: Senio valley hills; calcareous clays and sands, about 100 to 300 m.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Romagna DOC, one of 16 now listed (the original 12 of 2011 plus Imola, Coriano, San Clemente and Verucchio; San Vicinio has become Mercato Saraceno). A Romagna Sangiovese with a sottozona name needs at least 95% Sangiovese, at most 9 t/ha and 12.5% potential alcohol (13% for Riserva). The Riserva is released only from 1 September of the third year after the harvest, with two months in bottle documented.

appellations.name: Imola
appellations.village: Fontanelice, Borgo Tossignano, Casalfiumanese, Dozza, Castel San Pietro Terme, Ozzano dell'Emilia
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese (at least 95% for a sottozona wine)
appellations.summary: The newest western sottozona, in the Santerno and Sillaro valleys above Imola. Records from the late 18th century already describe Sangiovese as typical here, and an 1880 survey made it the second variety of Imola after Albana. The disciplinare backs the claim with numbers: the 2010 farm census counted 3,932 ha of vineyard in the province of Bologna, 1,039 ha (26%) of them Sangiovese, and 70% of that south of the Via Emilia, in the Imola hills.
appellations.terroir: Santerno and Sillaro valley hills south of the Via Emilia; clays, sands and spungone.
appellations.nerd_note: Dozza, inside the sottozona, houses the Enoteca Regionale dell'Emilia-Romagna in its medieval fortress.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Romagna DOC, one of 16 now listed (the original 12 of 2011 plus Imola, Coriano, San Clemente and Verucchio; San Vicinio has become Mercato Saraceno). A Romagna Sangiovese with a sottozona name needs at least 95% Sangiovese, at most 9 t/ha and 12.5% potential alcohol (13% for Riserva). The Riserva is released only from 1 September of the third year after the harvest, with two months in bottle documented.

appellations.name: Coriano
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese (at least 95% for a sottozona wine)
appellations.summary: The commune of Coriano plus a strip of Rimini, in the low hills behind the Riviera. San Patrignano, the rehabilitation community whose winery helped prove the area's potential, is in Coriano. Sangiovese was widely grown in the Rimini area until 1860, then abandoned for its low alcohol and later replanted. Coriano covers the land just behind the sea, and the disciplinare credits its grey clays and good exposure with more structured Sangiovese suited to ageing.
appellations.terroir: Low hills a few kilometres from the Adriatic; clays and sands, warm with sea breezes.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Romagna DOC, one of 16 now listed (the original 12 of 2011 plus Imola, Coriano, San Clemente and Verucchio; San Vicinio has become Mercato Saraceno). A Romagna Sangiovese with a sottozona name needs at least 95% Sangiovese, at most 9 t/ha and 12.5% potential alcohol (13% for Riserva). The Riserva is released only from 1 September of the third year after the harvest, with two months in bottle documented.

appellations.name: San Clemente
appellations.village: San Clemente, Montescudo-Montecolombo, Misano Adriatico, San Giovanni in Marignano, Montefiore Conca, Gemmano, Morciano di Romagna, Saludecio, Mondaino, Montegridolfo
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese (at least 95% for a sottozona wine)
appellations.summary: The Conca valley hills south of Rimini, excluding the land below the SS 16 coastal road. A Sangiovese-only sottozona on the border with the Marche. The disciplinare describes San Clemente as the hottest part of the Rimini hills, with gypsum and more colourful clays, giving structured wines that keep good acid tension.
appellations.terroir: Conca valley hills; clays and sands, warm, close to the sea.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Romagna DOC, one of 16 now listed (the original 12 of 2011 plus Imola, Coriano, San Clemente and Verucchio; San Vicinio has become Mercato Saraceno). A Romagna Sangiovese with a sottozona name needs at least 95% Sangiovese, at most 9 t/ha and 12.5% potential alcohol (13% for Riserva). The Riserva is released only from 1 September of the third year after the harvest, with two months in bottle documented.

appellations.name: Verucchio
appellations.village: Verucchio, Santarcangelo di Romagna, Poggio Torriana, Casteldelci, Maiolo, Novafeltria, Pennabilli, San Leo, Sant'Agata Feltria, Talamello
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese (at least 95% for a sottozona wine)
appellations.summary: The Marecchia valley from Santarcangelo up to the high Montefeltro. Seven of its communes (including San Leo and Pennabilli) moved from the Marche to Emilia-Romagna in 2009 after a referendum, so the sottozona includes land that was in another region until recently. On the Valmarecchia slopes, the disciplinare says, Sangiovese gives easier-drinking, more immediate wines than in the other Rimini sottozone.
appellations.terroir: Marecchia valley: low hills near Santarcangelo and Verucchio, steeper, cooler Montefeltro uplands above.
appellations.nerd_note: Verucchio was the cradle of the Malatesta family, lords of Rimini.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Romagna DOC, one of 16 now listed (the original 12 of 2011 plus Imola, Coriano, San Clemente and Verucchio; San Vicinio has become Mercato Saraceno). A Romagna Sangiovese with a sottozona name needs at least 95% Sangiovese, at most 9 t/ha and 12.5% potential alcohol (13% for Riserva). The Riserva is released only from 1 September of the third year after the harvest, with two months in bottle documented.

appellations.name: Cialla
appellations.grapes: Ribolla Gialla, Verduzzo Friulano, Refosco dal Peduncolo Rosso, Schioppettino; Bianco and Rosso blends (Picolit allowed in the Bianco)
appellations.summary: Cialla is a small, steep, wooded valley in the commune of Prepotto, close to the Slovenian border, and the most demanding subzone in Friuli. It exists largely because of one family: Paolo and Dina Rapuzzi bought land here in 1970, founded Ronchi di Cialla, and helped rescue Schioppettino from near-extinction. The subzone allows only native grapes (Ribolla Gialla, Verduzzo Friulano, Refosco and Schioppettino, plus Bianco and Rosso blends), with yields of 8 t/ha for whites and just 6 t/ha for reds, and long minimum release dates: January of the third year after the harvest for Refosco and Schioppettino. Wines must be bottled in glass of up to 5 litres with cork; Riserva needs four years.
appellations.terroir: A narrow side valley north of Prepotto, from about 200 m up to the road to Castelmonte; ponca (marl and sandstone flysch) terraces surrounded by woods; cool, wet and late.
appellations.nerd_note: Cialla's annex is the only one in the Colli Orientali that requires a cork stopper, and it allows small barrels for ageing.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Friuli Colli Orientali DOC with its own annex: native varieties only, 6 t/ha for reds and 8 t/ha for whites, small barrels allowed, Riserva after four years from 1 January after the harvest.

appellations.name: Schioppettino di Prepotto
match: Friuli Colli Orientali Schioppettino di Prepotto
appellations.grapes: Schioppettino at least 85% (95% for vineyards planted after the rules were published)
appellations.summary:
Prepotto, the commune that runs along the Judrio river on the Slovenian border, is Schioppettino's homeland, and this subzone is reserved for that one grape. Schioppettino (Ribolla Nera) gives medium-bodied, peppery, wild-berry reds with fresh acidity; the name may refer to the 'little gunshot' of its crisp berries or of the lively wines once refermented in bottle. The rules exclude the Cialla valley (which has its own subzone) and damp or shady land, require hand harvesting, at least 4,500 vines per hectare, 7 t/ha, 12% potential alcohol and at least 12 months in wood; release is from September of the second year after the harvest, and the Riserva from September of the fourth.

Producers in the commune include Vigna Petrussa, Ronco dei Pini, La Viarte, Grillo Iole and Colli di Poianis.
appellations.terroir: Ponca (marl and sandstone flysch) hills along the Judrio valley, about 100 to 300 m; mild, with cool air from the Julian Prealps.
appellations.nerd_note: Superiore is explicitly not allowed for Schioppettino di Prepotto, and the wine must go into a dark Bordeaux bottle.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Friuli Colli Orientali DOC for Schioppettino only, from the commune of Prepotto outside Cialla.

appellations.name: Rosazzo
match: Friuli Colli Orientali Pignolo di Rosazzo
Friuli Colli Orientali Ribolla Gialla di Rosazzo
appellations.village: Manzano, Corno di Rosazzo, San Giovanni al Natisone
appellations.grapes: Pignolo (Pignolo di Rosazzo) or Ribolla Gialla (Ribolla Gialla di Rosazzo), at least 85%
appellations.summary:
Two subzones of the Colli Orientali share one small area around the Abbey of Rosazzo, straddling Manzano, Corno di Rosazzo and San Giovanni al Natisone: Pignolo di Rosazzo and Ribolla Gialla di Rosazzo. The abbey's vineyards are where Pignolo, a dark, tannic and long-lived native red, survived near-extinction in the late 20th century; the rules call it the most aristocratic wine of the denomination, able to live well beyond ten years, and it may only be released from 1 November of the fourth year after the harvest. Ribolla Gialla di Rosazzo is the fresh, citrusy, tightly knit native white of the same hills. Both are capped at 8 t/ha with at least 3,500 vines per hectare.

The separate Rosazzo DOCG, for white blends led by Friulano, covers a wider area around the abbey; Livio Felluga, which manages the abbey's vineyards, Ronco delle Betulle and Le Vigne di Zamò are key names.
appellations.terroir: A compact block of ponca hills around the Abbey of Rosazzo, about 100 to 200 m; well ventilated, warm for the Colli Orientali.
appellations.nerd_note: Two different subzones (one red, one white) share exactly the same boundary, drawn along streams and farm tracks around the abbey.
appellations.classification: Area of the Friuli Colli Orientali sottozone 'Pignolo di Rosazzo' and 'Ribolla Gialla di Rosazzo', each with its own annex; distinct from the Rosazzo DOCG.

appellations.name: Refosco di Faedis
match: Friuli Colli Orientali Refosco di Faedis
appellations.village: Faedis, Nimis, Attimis, Torreano, Povoletto, Tarcento
appellations.grapes: Refosco Nostrano at least 85% (95% in new vineyards)
appellations.summary: The northern subzone of the Colli Orientali, for Refosco Nostrano, a local Refosco distinct from the more common Refosco dal Peduncolo Rosso, grown in the hills of Faedis, Nimis, Attimis, Torreano, Povoletto and Tarcento under the Julian Prealps. The rules allow 8 t/ha with at least 4,000 vines per hectare, and a Riserva after three years. The wines are deep-coloured, high in acidity and wild-berried.
appellations.terroir: Northern Colli Orientali, ponca and marl hills toward the Prealps; cooler and wetter than the southern hills.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Friuli Colli Orientali DOC for Refosco Nostrano.

appellations.name: Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle
match: Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle
Valle d'Aosta Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle
Vallée d'Aoste Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle
appellations.grapes: Prié Blanc 100%
appellations.summary:
The highest subzone of the valley and one of the highest vineyards in Europe, on the left bank of the Dora Baltea in Morgex and La Salle, below Mont Blanc, where the DOC zone runs up to 1,300 m. Prié Blanc, an ancient local white, ripens in barely five months, and many vines are on their own roots, trained on low pergolas (topie) held up by stone pillars so the grapes catch heat from the ground. The wines are pale, light and saline, with green apple and alpine herbs, and are also made as metodo classico.

Cave Mont Blanc, the cooperative of Morgex, makes most of it; Ermes Pavese is the leading independent grower.
appellations.terroir: Left bank of the Dora Baltea from the La Salle-Avise boundary to Pré-Saint-Didier, up to 1,300 m (vines mostly 900 to 1,200 m); sandy, stony morainic soils; long winters and frost risk.
producers: Cave Mont Blanc de Morgex et La Salle
appellations.nerd_note: Prié Blanc is one of the few European varieties still commonly grown ungrafted: phylloxera never thrived in Morgex's cold, sandy soils.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of the Valle d'Aosta / Vallée d'Aoste DOC, one of seven historic names (each with its own grape rules and delimitation in the disciplinare) that may follow the regional denomination on the label.

appellations.name: Enfer d'Arvier
appellations.grapes: Petit Rouge at least 85%
appellations.summary: 'Arvier's hell' is a tiny, sun-trapping amphitheatre of terraces above the village of Arvier, on both banks of the Dora Baltea at the mouth of the Valgrisenche, where the rock walls reflect so much heat that it feels infernal in summer. The wine is at least 85% Petit Rouge: deep ruby, with violets, wild cherries and a hint of almond. The Co-Enfer cooperative makes most of it.
appellations.terroir: Terraced slopes in the commune of Arvier (Monbet, Bouse, Sorpier and the left-bank slope toward Saint-Nicolas), roughly 750 to 900 m; south-facing, warm, rocky.
appellations.nerd_note: Enfer d'Arvier is one of Italy's smallest subzones: a single commune's sunniest terraces.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of the Valle d'Aosta / Vallée d'Aoste DOC, one of seven historic names (each with its own grape rules and delimitation in the disciplinare) that may follow the regional denomination on the label.

appellations.name: Torrette
appellations.village: Saint-Pierre, Villeneuve, Aymavilles, Sarre, Aosta, Quart and others
appellations.grapes: Petit Rouge at least 70%
appellations.summary: The largest red subzone of the valley, around Aosta from Quart to Villeneuve and Introd. Petit Rouge (at least 70%) gives supple, fragrant reds with cherry and violet; the best, from Les Crêtes, Grosjean and Elio Ottin, often labelled Torrette Supérieur, have real depth.
appellations.terroir: Both banks of the Dora Baltea around Aosta, up to 800 m on the right bank and 1,000 m on the left; morainic and alluvial-fan soils, sunny and dry.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of the Valle d'Aosta / Vallée d'Aoste DOC, one of seven historic names (each with its own grape rules and delimitation in the disciplinare) that may follow the regional denomination on the label.

appellations.name: Nus
appellations.grapes: Vien de Nus and Petit Rouge at least 70% (Vien de Nus at least 40%); Nus Malvoisie from Pinot Grigio
appellations.summary: Nus, east of Aosta, has two curiosities. The red must contain at least 40% of the rare Vien de Nus. The white, Nus Malvoisie, is made from Pinot Grigio (known here as Malvoisie) and is famous as a passito (flétri) from grapes dried after harvest, amber, honeyed and long.
appellations.terroir: Left bank from the Verrayes-Nus boundary to Aosta, up to 850 m, plus the Fénis right bank up to 650 m; sunny, dry slopes.
appellations.nerd_note: 'Malvoisie' in Nus is Pinot Grigio, not Malvasia: an old case of a borrowed name.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of the Valle d'Aosta / Vallée d'Aoste DOC, one of seven historic names (each with its own grape rules and delimitation in the disciplinare) that may follow the regional denomination on the label.

appellations.name: Chambave
appellations.village: Chambave, Châtillon, Pontey, Saint-Vincent, Saint-Denis, Verrayes, Montjovet
appellations.grapes: Petit Rouge at least 70% (red); Moscato Bianco (Chambave Muscat)
appellations.summary: Chambave, in the central valley, is best known for its Moscato: Chambave Muscat, dry and aromatic, and Chambave Muscat Flétri, a sweet wine from dried grapes, one of the great Alpine stickies. The red is at least 70% Petit Rouge. La Crotta di Vegneron and La Vrille are leading names; the late Ezio Voyat made the Flétri famous.
appellations.terroir: Both banks around Chambave, up to 700 m on the right and 750 m on the left; warm, dry, sunny central valley.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of the Valle d'Aosta / Vallée d'Aoste DOC, one of seven historic names (each with its own grape rules and delimitation in the disciplinare) that may follow the regional denomination on the label.

appellations.name: Arnad-Montjovet
appellations.village: Arnad, Montjovet, Hône, Issogne, Champdepraz, Verrès, Challand-Saint-Victor
appellations.grapes: Nebbiolo at least 70%
appellations.summary: The lower valley's second Nebbiolo subzone, between Hône and Montjovet, at least 70% Nebbiolo (locally Picotendro) with local reds. The wines are firm and fragrant, lighter than Donnas. Arnad is also famous for its lard (Lard d'Arnad DOP), cured in chestnut-wood tubs. La Kiuva, the Arnad cooperative, is the main producer.
appellations.terroir: Both banks between Hône and Montjovet, up to 600 m on the right and 700 m on the left; granite-gneiss terraces.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of the Valle d'Aosta / Vallée d'Aoste DOC, one of seven historic names (each with its own grape rules and delimitation in the disciplinare) that may follow the regional denomination on the label.

appellations.name: Donnas
appellations.grapes: Nebbiolo at least 85%
appellations.summary: The gateway subzone from Piedmont and the valley's first DOC (1971), in Donnas, Pont-Saint-Martin, Perloz and Bard. Nebbiolo (at least 85%) grows on pergolas over granite terraces that continue straight into Carema; the wines are pale, firm and perfumed and age at least two years. The Caves Coopératives de Donnas, founded in 1971, make almost all of it.
appellations.terroir: Left-bank hillsides above the SS 26 up to 700 m, plus the Valbona alluvial fan in Donnas on the right bank; granite and gneiss terraces with stone pillars and pergolas.
appellations.nerd_note: The Roman road to Gaul passes through Donnas, cut into the rock, with a carved milestone still in place among the vineyards.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of the Valle d'Aosta / Vallée d'Aoste DOC, one of seven historic names (each with its own grape rules and delimitation in the disciplinare) that may follow the regional denomination on the label.

appellations.name: Jerzu
appellations.grapes: Cannonau (Grenache) at least 85%
appellations.summary: Jerzu, in the Ogliastra on Sardinia's east side, is a village of steep vineyards below the limestone tacchi (table mountains), with the subzone extending to Cardedu on the coast. Cannonau has been the village's living for generations, and the Antichi Poderi di Jerzu cooperative makes most of the wine: ripe, spicy and generous, with the grip of the mountain sites. Ageing and bottling must take place inside the subzone.
appellations.terroir: Slopes from near the coast at Cardedu up to the terraces below the tacchi of Jerzu, granite and schist with limestone above; hot, dry summers and sea breezes.
appellations.nerd_note: The Ogliastra around Jerzu is one of the world's 'blue zones' of exceptional longevity, where the daily glass of Cannonau is part of local lore.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Cannonau di Sardegna DOC (one of three: Oliena or Nepente di Oliena, Jerzu, Capo Ferrato). Ageing and bottling must take place inside the subzone, unlike the island-wide DOC, and bag-in-box or other alternatives to glass are not allowed.

appellations.name: Oliena
match: Cannonau di Sardegna Nepente di Oliena
appellations.grapes: Cannonau (Grenache) at least 85%
appellations.summary: Oliena lies at the foot of Monte Corrasi and the limestone Supramonte near Nuoro, and its Cannonau has a literary nickname: Gabriele D'Annunzio called it 'Nepente di Oliena', after the nepenthe, Homer's drug of forgetfulness, and the subzone may use either name. It covers the whole commune of Oliena and part of Orgosolo. The wines are dark, warm and herbal, with the firmness of mountain fruit. The Cantina di Oliena cooperative and Gostolai are leading producers.
appellations.terroir: Slopes below the Supramonte limestone around Oliena, roughly 200 to 600 m; limestone and granite soils, dry, sunny and windy.
appellations.nerd_note: D'Annunzio's tribute made Oliena's Cannonau one of the few Italian wines with a nickname written into the rules: 'Oliena o Nepente di Oliena'.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Cannonau di Sardegna DOC (one of three: Oliena or Nepente di Oliena, Jerzu, Capo Ferrato). Ageing and bottling must take place inside the subzone, unlike the island-wide DOC, and bag-in-box or other alternatives to glass are not allowed.

appellations.name: Capo Ferrato
appellations.village: Castiadas, Muravera, San Vito, Villaputzu, Villasimius
appellations.grapes: Cannonau (Grenache) at least 85%
appellations.summary: The only subzone in the south of the island, on the south-east coast in Castiadas, Muravera, San Vito, Villaputzu and Villasimius, named after the headland of Capo Ferrato. Warm, maritime and lower than the mountain subzones, it gives rounder, riper Cannonau. Cantina Castiadas, the local cooperative, is the main producer. Capo Ferrato is also the only subzone that cannot be called Classico: that mention is reserved to the provinces of Nuoro and Ogliastra, and the Sarrabus coast lies in the south.
appellations.terroir: Coastal hills and plains of the Sarrabus, granite sands and alluvium; hot and dry, tempered by the sea.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Cannonau di Sardegna DOC (one of three: Oliena or Nepente di Oliena, Jerzu, Capo Ferrato). Ageing and bottling must take place inside the subzone, unlike the island-wide DOC, and bag-in-box or other alternatives to glass are not allowed.

appellations.name: Casauria
appellations.village: Tocco da Casauria, Castiglione a Casauria, Bolognano, Popoli, Torre de' Passeri, Alanno and other communes of the province of Pescara
appellations.grapes: Montepulciano (90 to 100% in the subzones)
appellations.summary: The inland Pescara valley between the Maiella and the Gran Sasso, around the Benedictine abbey of San Clemente a Casauria (founded 871). As a subzone of the DOC (also called Terre di Casauria) it required 100% Montepulciano, at most 9.5 t/ha, vineyards no higher than 600 m and at least 18 months of ageing with nine in wood. In November 2025 the area became its own DOCG, Casauria, Italy's 79th, so the subzone is being superseded. Tiberio, Zaccagnini and Valle Reale are among the producers within its communes.
appellations.terroir: Inland, foothill Pescara valley, about 200 to 600 m; clay-limestone and sandy-clay hills; strong day-night swings from the two massifs.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC with its own annex (version of the rules in force in early 2025). The original five subzones (Casauria, Terre dei Vestini, Alto Tirino, Terre dei Peligni, Teate) allow a base wine and Riserva from tightly drawn areas. Casauria was promoted to a separate DOCG (EU registration 11 November 2025).

appellations.name: Terre dei Vestini
appellations.village: Loreto Aprutino, Pianella, Penne, Moscufo, Città Sant'Angelo, Collecorvino, Spoltore and other communes of the province of Pescara
appellations.grapes: Montepulciano (90 to 100% in the subzones)
appellations.summary: The coastal and inner hills of the province of Pescara between the Adriatic and the Gran Sasso, named after the ancient Vestini people. Vineyards lie mostly between 200 and 500 m; the subzone allows up to 10 t/ha and requires 18 months of ageing with nine in wood. The area around Loreto Aprutino is one of Abruzzo's most celebrated for Montepulciano: Valentini's legendary cellar is here, and Torre dei Beati is a leading estate.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone hills from near the sea to the Gran Sasso foothills, 200 to 500 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Loreto Aprutino's Valentini, perhaps Abruzzo's most famous estate, sits inside Terre dei Vestini but does not use the subzone name.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC with its own annex (version of the rules in force in early 2025). The original five subzones (Casauria, Terre dei Vestini, Alto Tirino, Terre dei Peligni, Teate) allow a base wine and Riserva from tightly drawn areas.

appellations.name: Alto Tirino
appellations.village: Capestrano, Ofena, Villa Santa Lucia degli Abruzzi
appellations.grapes: Montepulciano (90 to 100% in the subzones)
appellations.summary: A small mountain basin in the province of L'Aquila: the plain of Ofena, nicknamed 'the oven of Abruzzo' for its summer heat, ringed by mountains, with surrounding slopes in Capestrano and Villa Santa Lucia. The subzone caps yields at 9 t/ha and requires 12 months of ageing; vineyards must lie between about 300 and 600 m. Hot days and very cold nights give deep colour and fresh acidity.
appellations.terroir: Intermontane basin of Ofena at 300 to 600 m, below the Gran Sasso; calcareous gravels and clays; extreme day-night swings.
appellations.nerd_note: Ofena's basin is called 'il forno d'Abruzzo', the oven of Abruzzo, though it lies among the highest mountains of the Apennines.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC with its own annex (version of the rules in force in early 2025). The original five subzones (Casauria, Terre dei Vestini, Alto Tirino, Terre dei Peligni, Teate) allow a base wine and Riserva from tightly drawn areas.

appellations.name: Terre dei Peligni
appellations.village: Sulmona, Pratola Peligna, Vittorito, Raiano, Corfinio, Prezza, Bugnara, Introdacqua, Pacentro, Pettorano sul Gizio, Roccacasale
appellations.grapes: Montepulciano (90 to 100% in the subzones)
appellations.summary: The Valle Peligna around Sulmona, an inland basin between the Maiella and the Velino-Sirente, with vineyards between about 300 and 400 m. Up to 10 t/ha and 24 months of ageing with nine in wood. Cooler and more continental than the coast, it gives firmer, more aromatic Montepulciano. Pietrantonj at Vittorito and Praesidium at Prezza are the reference estates.
appellations.terroir: Intermontane basin of the Valle Peligna, 300 to 400 m (vines up to 600 m); alluvial gravels and clay-limestone slopes; continental climate.
appellations.nerd_note: Sulmona, at the centre of the subzone, was the birthplace of Ovid.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC with its own annex (version of the rules in force in early 2025). The original five subzones (Casauria, Terre dei Vestini, Alto Tirino, Terre dei Peligni, Teate) allow a base wine and Riserva from tightly drawn areas.

appellations.name: Teate
appellations.village: About 60 communes of the province of Chieti (Chieti, Ortona, Lanciano, Vasto, Tollo, Guardiagrele and others)
appellations.grapes: Montepulciano (90 to 100% in the subzones)
appellations.summary: Teate is the Latin name of Chieti, and the subzone covers about a third of the province, the heart of Abruzzo's wine production: coastal hills from the Foro to the Trigno, then the inner and foothill hills up to the Maiella. At least 90% Montepulciano, 11 t/ha and 21 months of ageing with nine in wood. Chieti province grows most of Abruzzo's Montepulciano, much of it through large cooperatives such as those of Tollo, Ortona and the Frentano coast.
appellations.terroir: Coastal and inland clay-limestone hills of the province of Chieti up to 600 m; warm, with sea breezes and Maiella air.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC with its own annex (version of the rules in force in early 2025). The original five subzones (Casauria, Terre dei Vestini, Alto Tirino, Terre dei Peligni, Teate) allow a base wine and Riserva from tightly drawn areas.

appellations.name: Terre di Chieti
appellations.village: Chieti, Francavilla al Mare, Tollo, Ortona, Lanciano, Vasto, Guardiagrele and the rest of the province's wine communes
appellations.grapes: Montepulciano (90 to 100% in the subzones)
appellations.summary: One of the provincial subzones created in the reform, covering the province of Chieti, which grows most of Abruzzo's Montepulciano. Only Superiore (released no earlier than 1 October after the harvest) and Riserva (24 months, six in wood, released from 1 January of the third year) may carry the name. The reform built a pyramid: plain Montepulciano d'Abruzzo at the base (released from 1 February after the harvest), subzones with Superiore and Riserva above it, and the separate DOCGs (Colline Teramane, Terre Tollesi or Tullum, and since 2025 Casauria) at the top. Much of Abruzzo's Montepulciano is still trained on the traditional pergola abruzzese (tendone), though espaliers are spreading.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone hills from the Adriatic to the Maiella, up to 600 m.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC added in the reform that created three provincial subzones and one communal one, reserved for 'superiore' and 'riserva' wines: at least 90% Montepulciano, vineyards no higher than 600 m, Riserva aged 24 months with six in wood.

appellations.name: Terre Aquilane
appellations.village: Ofena, Capestrano, Sulmona, Pratola Peligna, Vittorito, Raiano, Fossa and the other wine communes of the province of L'Aquila
appellations.grapes: Montepulciano (90 to 100% in the subzones)
appellations.summary: The provincial subzone for the mountain province of L'Aquila (also 'Terre de L'Aquila'), joining the Ofena basin of Alto Tirino, the Valle Peligna and the Aterno and Roveto valleys. Superiore and Riserva only. The reform built a pyramid: plain Montepulciano d'Abruzzo at the base (released from 1 February after the harvest), subzones with Superiore and Riserva above it, and the separate DOCGs (Colline Teramane, Terre Tollesi or Tullum, and since 2025 Casauria) at the top. Much of Abruzzo's Montepulciano is still trained on the traditional pergola abruzzese (tendone), though espaliers are spreading.
appellations.terroir: Intermontane basins and valleys of L'Aquila province, 300 to 600 m; continental climate with very wide day-night swings.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC added in the reform that created three provincial subzones and one communal one, reserved for 'superiore' and 'riserva' wines: at least 90% Montepulciano, vineyards no higher than 600 m, Riserva aged 24 months with six in wood.

appellations.name: Colline Pescaresi
appellations.village: The wine communes of the province of Pescara
appellations.grapes: Montepulciano (90 to 100% in the subzones)
appellations.summary: The provincial subzone for Pescara, covering both the Vestini hills and the Casauria valley. Superiore and Riserva only. The reform built a pyramid: plain Montepulciano d'Abruzzo at the base (released from 1 February after the harvest), subzones with Superiore and Riserva above it, and the separate DOCGs (Colline Teramane, Terre Tollesi or Tullum, and since 2025 Casauria) at the top. Much of Abruzzo's Montepulciano is still trained on the traditional pergola abruzzese (tendone), though espaliers are spreading.
appellations.terroir: Pescara hills from the coast to the Gran Sasso and Maiella foothills, up to 600 m.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC added in the reform that created three provincial subzones and one communal one, reserved for 'superiore' and 'riserva' wines: at least 90% Montepulciano, vineyards no higher than 600 m, Riserva aged 24 months with six in wood.

appellations.name: San Martino sulla Marrucina
match: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo San Martino sulla Marrucina
appellations.grapes: Montepulciano (90 to 100% in the subzones)
appellations.summary: The only communal subzone: the hilltop village of San Martino sulla Marrucina at the foot of the Maiella in the province of Chieti, home of Masciarelli, the estate Gianni Masciarelli founded in 1981 that put modern Abruzzo on the map. Up to 12 t/ha, 12 months of ageing with six in wood, at least 4,000 vines per hectare.
appellations.terroir: Hills facing the Maiella in the province of Chieti, around 400 m; clay-limestone, with cool air from the mountain.
appellations.nerd_note: A whole subzone for one small hill village owes much to one estate: Masciarelli, maker of Villa Gemma and the Marina Cvetic range.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC added in the reform that created three provincial subzones and one communal one, reserved for 'superiore' and 'riserva' wines: at least 90% Montepulciano, vineyards no higher than 600 m, Riserva aged 24 months with six in wood.

appellations.name: Tinella
appellations.village: Costigliole d'Asti, Calosso, Castagnole delle Lanze, Coazzolo, Isola d'Asti
appellations.grapes: Barbera at least 90%
appellations.summary: Named after the Tinella stream, this subzone covers the hills of Costigliole d'Asti, Calosso, Castagnole delle Lanze and Coazzolo, plus the part of Isola d'Asti right of the Asti-Montegrosso road, on the border with the Langhe. Its marly-sandy clays and layered sandstones give Barbera of depth and freshness; the rules demand Guyot-trained vines on sunny slopes, 7 t/ha and two years of ageing with six months in wood and six in bottle.
appellations.terroir: South-west to south-east facing hills of clayey-sandy marl and stratified sandstone, about 200 to 400 m, between the Tanaro and the Langhe.
appellations.nerd_note: Calosso, inside Tinella, is the home of Gamba di Pernice, a rare local red named for the partridge-red colour of its stalks.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Barbera d'Asti DOCG, usable only for Barbera d'Asti Superiore: at least 90% Barbera, 7 t/ha (49 hl/ha), 12.5% potential alcohol, Guyot-trained vines on sunny hillsides facing south-east to south-west, and 24 months of ageing from 1 October after the harvest, with at least six in wood and six in bottle. The vintage is compulsory and only cork closures are allowed.

appellations.name: Colli Astiani
appellations.village: Asti (Montemarzo, San Marzanotto), Isola d'Asti, Mongardino, Vigliano d'Asti, Montegrosso d'Asti, Montaldo Scarampi, Rocca d'Arazzo, Azzano d'Asti
appellations.grapes: Barbera at least 90%
appellations.summary: The hills just south of Asti, from the city's own frazioni of Montemarzo and San Marzanotto through Mongardino, Vigliano, Montegrosso, Montaldo Scarampi, Rocca d'Arazzo and Azzano, plus the left side of Isola d'Asti; also labelled 'Astiano'. The rules mirror Tinella's: 90% Barbera, 7 t/ha, two years of ageing from 1 October with six months in wood and six in bottle, south-facing hillsides only.
appellations.terroir: Clayey-sandy marl and sandstone hills south of Asti and the Tanaro, about 150 to 350 m.
appellations.nerd_note: When Nizza left to become its own DOCG, Tinella and Colli Astiani remained as Barbera d'Asti's only subzones.
appellations.classification: Sottozona of Barbera d'Asti DOCG, usable only for Barbera d'Asti Superiore: at least 90% Barbera, 7 t/ha (49 hl/ha), 12.5% potential alcohol, Guyot-trained vines on sunny hillsides facing south-east to south-west, and 24 months of ageing from 1 October after the harvest, with at least six in wood and six in bottle. The vintage is compulsory and only cork closures are allowed.

appellations.name: Classico
match: Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi Classico
Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi Classico Superiore
appellations.village: Cupramontana, Staffolo, Montecarotto, San Paolo di Jesi, Serra de' Conti, Maiolati Spontini, Castelplanio, Apiro, Arcevia and others
appellations.grapes: Verdicchio at least 85%
appellations.summary:
The Classico area is 'the oldest original zone' of Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi: the whole delimited area except the land left (north) of the Misa river and the communes of Ostra and Senigallia toward the sea. In practice it is the hill country of the Esino valley around the walled castelli: Cupramontana (the self-styled capital of Verdicchio), Staffolo, San Paolo di Jesi, Maiolati Spontini and Castelplanio on the right bank, Montecarotto, Serra de' Conti and Arcevia on the left.

Classico may yield 14 t/ha, Classico Superiore only 11 t/ha with higher alcohol; Riserva is a separate DOCG. The rules also list about a hundred menzioni geografiche, from Balciana (Sartarelli's late-harvest cru in Poggio San Marcello) and Coroncino in Staffolo to Villa Bucci in Montecarotto. Bucci, Sartarelli, Colonnara, Umani Ronchi, Pievalta, Fattoria Coroncino, Vallerosa Bonci, Andrea Felici and La Distesa are among the defining producers.
appellations.terroir: Hills of 150 to 550 m on both banks of the Esino. The right bank (Cupramontana, Staffolo) is higher, on calcareous clay and limestone marl, and gives taut, long-lived wines; the left bank (Montecarotto, Serra de' Conti) has more clay and sand and gives broader wines. The Adriatic is about 30 km away.
appellations.nerd_note: Cupramontana's grape festival, the Sagra dell'Uva, held every October since 1928, is one of the oldest in Italy.
appellations.classification: Geographic qualification 'Classico' of Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi DOC (and Classico Superiore), reserved for the oldest part of the zone as defined in article 3 of the disciplinare.
